The US-Iran war has upended global crude trade flows not just by limiting the volume of oil reaching the market, but also by creating a structural deficit in the specific type of crudes that the world's more complex refineries need most.

Not all barrels are created equal, as is illustrated in the Platts Periodic Table of Oil, which highlights 150 of the key crude streams in the global oil market.

When it comes to medium and heavy sour barrels, the Middle East is the primary source, with grades including Saudi Arabia's Arab Medium and Arab Heavy, Iraq's Basrah Heavy, and Kuwaiti, Omani and Iranian crudes forming the staple diet of many complex refineries configured precisely for these grades' API gravities, sulfur levels and yields #oott https://t.co/sscYEUhHtf

Copper: Pushback on the feed argues mine supply downgrades are old news and China property drag caps the upside. Fair points on macro headwinds not fading that.

Let’s look under the hood. Some guys claim negative spot TCs are just a noise metric since refined cathode isn't visibly starving yet. Wrong. The real asymmetric driver is the violent regional inventory dislocation.

This rally was never a China front run. US physical imports are ripping. August ran ~200kt, and vessel tracking already logs 77kt locked for September.

GS models cumulative YTD US excess imports at a massive ~730k MT. Meanwhile in China, despite brutal inventory draws (upstream -41% y/y, downstream -8% y/y), SHFE open interest is nowhere near stretched.

Ex-China looks just as clean. Vol is getting hammered, options positioning is sitting at an uncrowded 3/10, and futures longs are around 4/10. Nobody is max long flat price; desk exposure is parked in polite LME spread duration.

Crucially smelters can’t cleanly roll their con hedges into prompt without eating toxic negative carry against low headline TCs, blowing out LME spreads into persistent backwardation flares.

Secondary rod run rates are still down 50% YoY on extreme scrap starvation.

Fabricators have zero choice but to melt virgin cathode to offset the scrap hole, artificially propping up apparent demand way above actual baseline end-use consumption.

Don’t expect tariff threats to get walked back. The current playbook—US sucking in massive physical units tariff-free, lubricated by Wall Street cash and carry financing—is Washington’s wet dream. If imports slow, critical mineral security concerns could easily bring tariff rhetoric back into focus.

China property is cooked? Sure consensus agrees. But China didn’t print this ATH, and they won't dictate the next leg either. It is driven by structural ex-US deficits from aggressive US inventory absorption, combined with cathode substitution due to scrap exhaustion.

China's onshore buffers are melting. When their domestic inventory cushion completely zeroes out and forced buyers have to chase prompt imports, where does the tape clear?

Not trading daily chop, but structurally this cycle’s legs are way longer than the timeline thinks.

Platinum is in a feisty mood after the WPIC, in its 2026 outlook, highlighted that the first - albeit small - surplus since 2022 is being driven by reduced financial demand, something we know can change on a dime if momentum returns. Platinum is up 5% on the day, touching a three-month high at USD 1,918.

Importantly, the WPIC stressed that inventories remain critically depleted following three consecutive years of significant deficits, including a revised 2025 shortfall of more than 1.4 Moz. As a result, above-ground stocks are expected to cover just 3.4 months of global demand by the end of 2026.

In other words, the projected surplus may look comfortable on paper, but the underlying inventory cushion remains exceptionally thin.

Gold rangebound as weaker dollar offsets rate-hike and inflation risks.
Gold traders - and the algorithmic programmes that account for a significant share of day-to-day activity - are currently struggling to determine which of several competing themes will ultimately set the tone, overall keeping prices rangebound around USD 4,400. As the charts below illustrate, the clearest headwind has come from rising rate-hike expectations and higher bond yields, increasing the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset such as gold.

Against this, a softer dollar has provided support, while underlying investment demand through ETFs and futures has so far remained relatively resilient. Geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated with the latest Middle East flareup helping to maintain gold’s appeal as a portfolio diversifier, limiting the downside despite the renewed pressure from yields.

With next week’s FOMC decision currently viewed as close to a coin toss between unchanged rates and a hike, the August CPI and PPI releases later this week could prove decisive. A hotter inflation print would likely reinforce rate-hike expectations and keep yields elevated, while softer data could quickly unwind some of the recent hawkish repricing as the window for a hike in my opinion then shuts until after the November Midterms. Either way, the inflation data may provide the catalyst that breaks gold out of its current tug-of-war and sets the direction ahead of the September meeting.

OPEC crude production fell by 900,000 b/d last month to 19.9 mb/d, almost 10 mb/d below pre-war levels, and partly reversing the increase that followed the signing of the now-failed MOU. The decline was primarily driven by a 1.1 mb/d slump in Saudi output amid attacks on pipeline infrastructure, only partly offset by increases from Iraq, Kuwait, Nigeria and Venezuela, the latter reaching an eight-year high at 1.2 mb/d. (Source: Bloomberg production survey).
